blocks.text: Objective 4.1 is a catalog of controls. The exam does not ask you to recite products, but to **choose the right control for a given risk**. Start with the techniques that reduce the attack surface even before any detection.

blocks.field: Dividing the network into zones to limit lateral movement. One compromised service must not grant access to all others.

blocks.note: Trust / DMZ / Untrust zones and segmentation

blocks.field: Reducing the attack surface: disabling unnecessary services, applying patches, configuring secure baselines, removing default accounts.
Least privilege, separation of duties, and authentication before any access to a resource.
Executing suspicious code or files in an isolated environment to observe behavior without risking production.

blocks.note: System controls, endpoints, and isolated execution

blocks.text: Deception does not protect by blocking, but by **early detection**: decoys are placed that have no legitimate reason to be touched. Any contact with them is a high-value signal.

blocks.field: Decoy system that simulates a vulnerable target to attract attackers and record their techniques.

head: Decoy
Nature
Detected Signal
rows: Opening or copying of the file

blocks.note: Official objectives — honeynet, honeyfile, honeytoken, and canary absent from the 4 books

blocks.text: Honeynet, honeyfile, honeytoken, and canary account are required in **§4.1**; only honeypot is described in the provided books. These variants are written from the objectives, without attribution to a book.

blocks.note: Deception and application controls in the SOC

blocks.q: An attacker attempts to use a fake credential planted in a configuration file. Which technique is this?
blocks.explain: A honeytoken is a fake credential or token: its use immediately reveals hostile activity.

items: Segmentation, hardening, access controls, and sandboxing reduce the surface before detection.
A honeypot is a decoy system; a honeynet is an entire network of decoys.
Honeyfile, honeytoken, and canary account detect use of specific baits.
Any interaction with a decoy is a high-confidence indicator.

title: IDS/IPS, Firewalls, and Network Access Control

blocks.text: The network control family is distinguished along two axes: **network vs. host** and **detection vs. prevention**. Once these two axes are mastered, the acronyms become obvious.
Detect or Prevent: IDS vs. IPS

right.title: IPS — Intrusion Prevention System
points: Placed inline in the traffic path.

blocks.note: IDS and IPS: detection, prevention, signatures, and anomalies

head: Control
Scope
Position
rows: Files, logs, and processes of a host

blocks.note: IDS/IPS, host agents, and security appliances

blocks.text: Classic trap: **IDS = detective**, **IPS = preventive**. A WIPS acts on wireless and can block a rogue access point.

items: **Rule-based firewall**: explicit allow/deny rules on IP, port, and protocol.
**Layer 4 / Layer 7 firewall**: filtering by port (Layer 4) or application content (Layer 7).
**Rate-limiting requests**: limits request count to counter abuse and floods.

blocks.field: Filters HTTP/HTTPS traffic at the application layer: SQL injection, cross-site scripting, request abuse. It protects the application, not the entire network.
Device that combines multiple functions (firewall, IPS, antivirus, web filtering, VPN) into a single appliance.

blocks.note: Official objectives — WAF and UTM absent from the 4 books

blocks.text: WAF and UTM are required in **§4.1** but absent from the provided books. These definitions come from the objectives and industry practice.

items: **Captive portals**: authentication before network access (guests, BYOD).
**802.1X**: port-level network authentication via a RADIUS server.
**Endpoint posture/compliance**: the device is accepted only if it complies with policy (patches, antivirus, encryption).

blocks.note: Detection tools, collection, and network controls

blocks.q: Which control blocks an HTTP request containing a SQL injection before it reaches the application?
blocks.explain: The WAF inspects HTTP application content and blocks web attacks; a NIDS would only see network traffic and prevent nothing.

items: IDS = out-of-path detection; IPS = inline prevention.
NIDS/NIPS = network; HIDS/HIPS = host; WIPS = wireless.
WAF = HTTP application filtering; UTM = multi-function appliance.
NAC: captive portal, 802.1X, and device compliance before access.

title: Endpoint, DLP, Email, and Code Security

blocks.text: Modern controls go beyond the firewall: they protect the **endpoint**, **outbound data**, **email**, and **code**. This is also the part of §4.1 most absent from the provided books.

blocks.field: Detects and removes known malware using signatures, supplemented by heuristic analysis.

head: Technology
Scope
Key Function
rows: Detects behaviors, enables isolation and response
Blocks copying or sending of sensitive data

blocks.field: Identifies, monitors, and blocks sensitive data in motion, at rest, or on the endpoint based on content rules.

blocks.note: Official objectives — DLP/EDR/XDR and DMARC/SPF/DKIM/BIMI written from objectives

blocks.text: EDR/XDR and DLP are required in **§4.1** but absent from the four books. Watch out for the error noted in SOC Notes: **EDR is an endpoint agent, not a next-generation firewall**.

head: Mechanism
Role
rows: Authorizes servers allowed to send for a domain (DNS record)
Cryptographic signature of the message, verifiable via public key published in DNS
SPF/DKIM alignment policy and failure handling (none/quarantine/reject) + reporting
Displays the verified brand logo in the email client

blocks.text: DMARC is **not a certificate**: it is a DNS policy record. It builds on SPF and DKIM. This corrects an error present in SOC Notes.

items: **Input validation**, **secure cookies**, and **static code analysis**: reduce application defects.
**Code signing**: sign binaries to guarantee origin and integrity.
**Secrets scanning**: detect hardcoded passwords and keys in repositories.
**Group Policy** (Windows): enforce passwords, lockout, and security settings.
**SELinux** (Linux): mandatory access control (MAC) that restricts even a compromised process.

blocks.note: Official objectives — code signing, secrets scanning, and SELinux absent from the 4 books
Windows infrastructure and system security policies

blocks.q: A developer committed an API key to a public repository. Which control should have stopped it?
blocks.explain: Secrets scanning analyzes code and repository history to spot hardcoded keys, tokens, and passwords.

items: EDR = endpoint agent; XDR = multi-source correlation; DLP = sensitive data control.
SPF authorizes sender, DKIM signs, DMARC enforces policy, BIMI displays logo.
Code signing, secrets scanning, and SELinux are objectives concepts outside the books.
Choose the control by layer: network, endpoint, application, or email.
